events.title: Margaret Schedel Music to Cure Parkinsons Guest Talk
events.description:
Dr. Margaret Schedel, a professor at Stony Brook University, presents “Listening to Data: Sound as a Data Source and a Display.” Her talk explores how sound can be used to understand and interpret data, a technique known as sonification. Schedel demonstrates how listening to data can reveal patterns and details that might be difficult to recognize through graphs and charts alone. She presents applications of this technology in fields ranging from astronomy to materials science and medicine. One major focus is her research on using music and artificial intelligence to help patients with Parkinson’s disease improve their walking. Through her project WeStep, Schedel demonstrates how changes in music can provide immediate feedback to patients, helping them recognize and correct irregular movements. She also highlights how combining sound with traditional visualizations makes scientific data more accessible and easier to understand. Ultimately, her presentation shows how listening to data opens new possibilities for scientific research, healthcare, and technology.

events.title: The Birth and Evolution of LLM Part 2
events.description:
In this workshop, we will continue our historical journey toward today's large language models, such as ChatGPT and Claude. Part 1 showed how far counting can go with Markov chains and N-grams, and where it fails: a counting model cannot handle word sequences it has never seen. In Part 2, we will start with Bengio's Neural Probabilistic Language Model (2003), one of the first neural network language models to outperform N-grams. We will then look at how context changed with RNNs (2010), attention (2014), and the Transformer (2017), the architecture behind today's LLMs. No background in computer science or AI is required, and Part 1 is helpful but not required. The difficult part is the idea that a word can be a list of numbers. Our journey covers roughly 2003 to today.

events.title: Systematic Review Incubator – Apply Now!
events.description:
Interested in conducting a systematic or scoping review but not sure where to start? Have an idea for a review but need structure, support, and accountability to see it through? Apply for the Systematic Review Incubator, a structured, cohort-based program designed to guide participants through the evidence synthesis process. With guidance from librarians with expertise in evidence synthesis, participants will work through the stages of the review process, from developing a research question and protocol to building comprehensive searches, screening studies, and synthesizing data. Participants can complete the initial five-month phase with a registered protocol and the foundational materials needed to conduct their review, or continue for up to 12 months to work toward a high-quality, submission-ready manuscript that follows established evidence synthesis methods and reporting guidelines. The program is open to members of the Stony Brook community, including students, faculty, clinicians, and staff. Undergraduate students must be in their junior year or above. Before applying, we strongly encourage you to watch the recording of our information session or review the presentation slides. Application Deadline: November 20, 2026 | Apply Now
